items.title: It’s raining lawsuits for Meta 👓
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks and Happy Fridayyyyy! ☀️

Data centres are finding a new way to win hearts: your kids’ school trips.

Industry groups are handing out data-centre-themed storybooks, colouring pages and science projects, while companies like Amazon and Sabey are taking students on facility tours.

One group even sponsored flag-making kits for 3,100 first-graders, complete with facts about the industry’s economic benefits.

Part of a broader push: as data centres face growing backlash over their huge energy needs and local impact, the industry is trying to get communities on its side by winning over the next generation.

It’s a tried-and-tested PR playbook used by industries like oil, gas and fast food: get into classrooms, tell your side of the story and shape how people see you.

Turns out, the next big data-centre recruit might still be learning their ABCs.

Indian markets fell for the third straight session on Thursday, with the Sensex and Nifty both closing lower.

FMCG, IT and energy stocks dragged markets down, while midcap and smallcap indices fell around 1%.

Meanwhile, Brent crude hovering around $112-113 a barrel and rising Middle East tensions are stoking inflation worries and keeping investors on edge.

💡Spotlight: A deal worth ₹770 crore for drone-detecting radars 🛡️

The Defence Ministry has signed a ₹770 crore deal with Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) to supply advanced radars to the Indian Army. However, despite the announcement, BEL shares fell more than 1%.

These radars can detect and track fighter jets and small, low-flying drones. They can also help prioritise threats so the Army can respond faster.

The need for such technology became clearer during Operation Sindoor, when Pakistan launched several waves of drones towards Indian military and civilian areas. Indian air defence systems intercepted many of them.

The radars are an upgraded version of an existing Indian system called Aslesha, developed by DRDO and manufactured by BEL.

The government says the deal will also support India’s domestic defence industry, including smaller companies involved in manufacturing radar equipment.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: India-Poland to double trade by 2030 🤝

India and Poland have agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy as the two countries look to turn their strategic partnership into actual projects.

The defence push: India has invited Polish companies to manufacture defence equipment in India through joint development and production.

The two sides have also proposed a dedicated defence industry dialogue to connect companies and identify commercially viable projects.

Space and nuclear energy: India and Poland also want their research institutions and companies to work more closely in space and nuclear energy.

They will also explore cooperation in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, quantum technology, critical minerals and battery recycling.

The business angle: the two countries have set a target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

Poland can act as a gateway for Indian companies looking to expand into Central and Eastern Europe. India, meanwhile, offers Polish companies a large consumer market, manufacturing base and skilled workforce.

The Ukraine context: Tusk’s visit comes as global efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war gather momentum.

Modi said India would continue supporting every meaningful effort to restore peace in Ukraine and West Asia.

Why Poland matters: Poland is one of Europe’s fastest-growing major economies and recently crossed the $1 trillion GDP mark. Its location also makes it an important manufacturing and logistics hub for companies looking to enter the wider European market.

Share

2. Swiggy’s growth comes with sides ☹️

A day after rival Eternal reported its results, Swiggy released its Q2 earnings. Revenue grew sharply and its overall loss narrowed, but losses in quick commerce continued to rise.

By the numbers (YoY):

  • Net loss: ₹922 crore, down from ₹1,092 crore

  • Revenue: ₹5,561 crore, up 54.4%

  • Operating loss, measured by EBITDA: ₹770 crore, down from ₹798 crore

  • Quick-commerce revenue: ₹1,306 crore, up 33.3%

  • Food-delivery revenue: ₹2,338 crore, up 21.6%

The expensive bit: Instamart brought in more revenue, but its losses reached ₹764 crore, compared with ₹739 crore a year earlier and ₹651 crore in the previous quarter.

Swiggy also added 69 dark stores, the local warehouses that fulfil quick-commerce orders. Its network now spans 1,240 stores across 133 cities.

Food delivery offered relief: the total value of food orders rose 18% to ₹10,054 crore. Adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating earnings, increased by ₹101 crore to ₹341 crore.

Market reaction: Swiggy shares fell 5% to an all-time low.

FYI: Eternal is now worth roughly five times as much on the stock market: ₹2.96 lakh crore versus Swiggy’s ₹58,000 crore. That gap was only a little over two times when Swiggy went public in November 2024.

Share

3. Meta’s past is proving expensive 🫣

Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in a case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The penalty follows a jury’s finding that the company misled Facebook users about how it protected their personal data and handled harmful content.

What happened: in 2018, Facebook disclosed that political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica had improperly obtained data belonging to as many as 87 million users.

The firm used it to build voter profiles and target political ads during the 2016 US election, when it worked for Donald Trump’s campaign.

In 2021, the state sued Facebook, alleging that it had misled users about who could access their data. The lawsuit also challenged its claims about tackling hate speech and misinformation, alleging that it tolerated harmful content when doing so benefited its business.

In September, a jury found Meta responsible for more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection law. Wednesday’s ruling put a price on those violations: $25 billion.

Meta’s response: the company called the lawsuit ‘a tax on speech’, arguing that the ruling makes doing business in New Mexico almost impossible.

It accused the state of mixing privacy concerns with questions about what people can say online and said it expects to win on appeal.

The bigger picture: this adds to Meta’s growing legal bills over privacy and child safety. Earlier this year, New Mexico secured another $942 million in penalties in a separate case involving young users’ safety on Facebook and Instagram.

Share

4. Why is Eternal building Dark.ai? 👀

Eternal is building an AI chatbot called Dark.ai, with plans to launch it globally by the end of 2026.

Deepinder Goyal claims encryption and user-controlled memory will prevent even Eternal from reading users’ conversations.

The company plans to use existing AI models and could charge for the service. But pricing is undecided, and its privacy claims remain unverified.

What does a food-delivery company see in private AI conversations? We unpack the technology, the business case and the questions Eternal still needs to answer.

Find Out Here

5. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

⚡️Kalpataru Projects International gained after it secured new domestic EPC orders worth ₹2,349 crore, taking total FY27 year-to-date order inflows past ₹22,000 crore.

💪🏻 SRF ended 1% higher after rebounding 7% from its intraday low as positive management commentary helped improve overall investor sentiment.

📈 Indian Hotels Company went up nearly 4% after it reported Q2 earnings that came in ahead of street expectations.

What went down ⬇️

👎🏻 PC Jeweller slipped nearly 2% despite a 58% rise in Q2 net profit year-on-year to ₹330.66 crore on higher sales.

🤒 KEI Industries fell 8% after the company’s cautious margin outlook raised concerns among investors about its future profit growth.

🫤 Oracle Financial Services Software slipped 4%, while Hindustan Petroleum Corporation also faced selling pressure ahead of its earnings announcement.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

🚢 Vessel contract: SEAMEC secured a $55 million contract with HAL Offshore to provide a vessel for ONGC’s offshore inspection, maintenance and repair work for around 1,225 days.

📊 Market expansion: NCDEX launched two new indices, NDEX and FINNDEX, marking its entry into equity and equity derivatives markets.

🏥 Healthcare funding: Rural healthcare startup CureBay raised around ₹100 crore in Pre-Series C funding led by IvyCap Ventures to expand across India and strengthen its AI capabilities.

🍔 Food delivery: Shiprocket entered the food delivery market with a direct-ordering model, helping restaurants reduce costs and manage orders through their own channels.

🤖 AI funding: DeepSeek raised $15 billion to expand its AI data centres and develop more open-source models, stepping up competition with leading US AI companies.

And that’s a wrap. Pour yourself an extra one this weekend. 🥳

We’ll be back like clockwork on Monday!

items.title: Musk meets Musk 🤝
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks!

Remember we had put up a poll a few days ago asking if you’d be interested in something new? Well, we’re working on it. We are cookin’ something.

Well, we’ve now created a space for you to sign up. Just drop your name and let us know, should we count you in?

Elsewhere on the internet, as if the wellness industry didn’t manipulate people enough already, a new Futurism article is flagging a disturbing new trend: apps being promoted by sobbing AI-generated women.

TikTok is filled with fake family drama, emotional texts from loved ones and sneaky app notifications, all designed to sell wellness tools.

From GLP-1 weight-loss trackers to mental health apps, these AI-generated sob stories often go undisclosed as ads. Yes, even your TikTok heartbreak could be sponsored content.

Some viewers are falling for the stories, while companies face questions over transparency.

One developer admitted the AI visuals should have been labelled, while another blamed unauthorised affiliates.

Our two cents: AI is supposed to take tasks off our plate, not add another one like figuring out what’s real and what’s just trying to sell us something.

Moving on, Dalal Street ended the day in the red, with both the Sensex and Nifty retreating sharply from their intraday highs.

IT stocks were the only bright spot, with the Nifty IT index closing in positive territory. Selling in banking, auto and realty stocks weighed on the benchmark indices, while defence stocks also declined sharply.

Meanwhile, the rupee strengthened to ₹94.49 against the US dollar, its highest level in six weeks, supported by RBI measures.

💡Spotlight: a cybersecurity wake-up call 🫤

India’s biggest lender, the State Bank of India (SBI), has disclosed a suspected cyber incident involving the exposure of customer records on the dark web.

What’s happening: SBI said a preliminary analysis of about 3,75,000 records found on the dark web identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information (PII).

The exposed information reportedly included customers’ registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses and residential addresses.

The bank said the incident had not materially affected its core operations, financial performance or business continuity.

Indian cybersecurity company eMudhra has also come under scrutiny.

The why: all eight security certificates it issued had a serious flaw. Researchers cracked their secret keys in less than a second.

Attackers could potentially have used those keys to pose as trusted websites and fool users into connecting to fake servers.

Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla have since moved to block the affected certificates, while Cloudflare and other software providers have released security fixes. So far, there is no evidence that attackers exploited the weakness.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: Eternal had a very busy Wednesday 👀

Eternal announced a MyGate investment, entered the AI race with Dark.ai and reported strong revenue growth but its shares still fell after profit missed expectations.

First, a ₹156 crore acquisition: the company will acquire a 5.4% stake in MyGate through a share-swap deal valued at around ₹156 crore.

MyGate is a technology platform used by gated communities to manage visitors, deliveries, security and communication between residents.

Eternal will not pay cash for the stake. Instead, it will give MyGate shareholders some of the shares it owns in advertising technology company Adonmo.

The why: MyGate gives Eternal another entry point into urban households. Its apps already reach consumers through food delivery, groceries, restaurant bookings and events. MyGate adds residential communities to that list.

Deepi goes dark with AI: Deepinder Goyal is also taking Eternal beyond food and quick commerce.

The company plans to launch Dark.ai, a privacy-focused AI assistant, globally by the end of 2026.

Dark.ai is being designed for people who want to use AI without worrying that their conversations, research or business ideas could be accessed or retained by someone else.

How it works: the assistant will use fine-tuned open-weight AI models running on Eternal’s own infrastructure. Conversations will be protected using end-to-end encryption.

Q2 earnings: Eternal also reported its Q2 FY27 earnings, with revenue and profit rising sharply. However, the shares fell because the company’s profit was much lower than analysts had expected.

By the numbers 📊:

  • Net profit: ₹125 crore, up 92% YoY

  • Revenue: ₹24,138 crore, up 78% YoY

  • Total expenses: ₹24,166 crore, up 75% YoY

  • Expected profit: around ₹250 crore

Eternal earned nearly twice as much profit as it did last year, but that ₹125 crore figure was only half of what the Street expected. That explains why the stock fell despite the impressive growth numbers.

A small catch: Eternal said its like-for-like revenue grew 58%, not 78%. The reported growth looks higher because Blinkit shifted to an inventory-led model, under which the full value of products sold is now counted as revenue.

Note: Blinkit now contributes the most reported revenue, although its accounting model makes a direct comparison with food delivery less straightforward.

Share

2. Welcome to Elon Musk’s multiverse 🚀

Elon Musk’s companies may be preparing for their biggest crossover yet.

SpaceX and Tesla have formed separate committees of independent directors to explore a possible merger. Musk, who runs both companies and owns large stakes in them, believes combining the two would be a “good idea”.

No deal has been agreed. Musk is not participating directly in the discussions because he sits on both sides of the table. The committees must now decide whether a merger makes financial and strategic sense for shareholders.

The why: on the surface, electric cars and rockets have little in common. Look deeper, and Musk sees the two companies as pieces of the same technology machine.

  • Tesla needs AI to power self-driving vehicles and humanoid robots. SpaceX is building large computing systems and already rents computing power to other AI companies.

  • Both companies require powerful, specialised chips. Developing some technology together could reduce duplication and speed up production.

  • Tesla is developing its Optimus humanoid robot, while SpaceX needs automation for factories, launch sites and possible operations in space.

  • Starlink’s satellite network could provide internet connections to Tesla vehicles, robots and other devices almost anywhere.

Tesla investors could help finance extremely expensive space and AI projects. SpaceX investors would inherit Tesla’s exposure to the competitive car industry, manufacturing problems and demand cycles.

Share

3. Why is Flipkart entering food delivery now? 👀

Flipkart is preparing to enter India’s food-delivery market, taking on Zomato and Swiggy with a proposed 10% restaurant commission, compared with the usual 20-25%.

Its new service, Eat-in by Minutes, is reportedly being tested with over 8,000 employees in Bengaluru.

But why food delivery now? As Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart expand into traditional e-commerce, Flipkart wants customers opening its app more frequently. Food delivery could help it achieve that, while its existing logistics network gives it a head start.

Amazon tried something similar and shut down its food-delivery business in 2022. Can Flipkart succeed where Amazon failed?

Full Story Here

4. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

💸 Transrail Lighting rallied 4% after the company announced that it had secured orders worth ₹927 crore.

🫡 L&T Technology Services surged over 10% after reporting Q2 net profit of ₹548 crore, up 66% from last year.

🏝️Mahindra Holidays and Resorts India gained after profit rose 11.8% to ₹19.95 crore and revenue increased 9.3% to ₹784 crore.

What went down ⬇️

🤒 ABB India fell up to 6% after parent company ABB Global released its latest quarterly business update.

🫤 Gallantt Ispat reported a 31.95% decline in Q2 profit to ₹60.5 crore, while revenue rose 13.1% year-on-year to ₹1,146 crore. Its shares tumbled over 7%.

👎🏻 Bajaj Finance slipped over 3%, emerging as the biggest Nifty loser amid investor concerns about the company’s margin outlook.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

📈 IPO plans: Carlsberg is preparing to file for an IPO of its India business, potentially raising up to $700 million.

🏗️ New orders: Kalpataru Projects International secured ₹2,349 crore in domestic EPC orders across power transmission, distribution and building construction.

🤖 IPO losses: Anthropic’s first-half net loss widened to $80.7 billion, largely due to accounting adjustments on convertible bonds, ahead of its planned November IPO.

📱Jio IPO: Jio Platforms’ ₹30,200 crore IPO saw its institutional investor portion subscribed nearly 2 times, after raising ₹8,110 crore from 212 anchor investors.

☀️ Solar acquisition: Transrail Lighting acquired a 49% stake in NOPL Pace Green Energy, which is developing a 990 MW solar portfolio in Maharashtra under the PM-KUSUM scheme.

⚡️Powering ahead: India’s core sector output grew 7.9% in September, a 30-month high, driven by coal production, electricity generation and refinery products.

That’s a wrap! Don’t let the weekday blues get to you.

items.title: India-US trade deal ‘very close’ 👀
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks!

Monday wasn’t kind to the markets. Dalal Street failed to sustain an early recovery and ended the session with significant losses.

The Sensex and Nifty declined more than 1% as private sector banks fell sharply after missing profit expectations for the July-September quarter.

💡 Spotlight: Sugar stocks turn bitter 🍬

Sugar stocks fell up to 6% on Monday after the government stopped sugar mills from using sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses to produce ethanol during the 2026-27 supply year.

Why the fall: ethanol is an important and often more profitable business for sugar companies. Mills could earlier choose between producing sugar or ethanol depending on which offered better returns.

The new rule removes that flexibility and could reduce earnings from ethanol plants.

The bigger picture: India’s sugar production is expected to remain under pressure following weak rainfall in Maharashtra and Karnataka.

With sugar prices already elevated during the festive season, the government is prioritising food supply over fuel production.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: India-US trade deal ‘very close’ 👀

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India for talks with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, with trade, energy and defence cooperation high on the agenda.

A trade deal, finally?: the long-running India-US trade negotiations were back in focus. Rubio said an agreement was “very, very close”, with only a few issues left to resolve.

He expressed optimism that the two countries would reach a deal soon, calling India an important commercial and strategic partner.

Why Venezuelan oil came up: Rubio called India a ‘refining superpower’, saying its refineries could process more Venezuelan crude as supplies increase.

Venezuela produces heavy crude, which requires specialised refining facilities. Rubio said Indian refineries had processed it before, while Indian companies already held rights to extract oil in Venezuela, creating opportunities to increase production.

He also said he would explore whether Reliance could refine more Venezuelan oil, pointing to its large refining capacity and previous experience with the country’s crude.

However, Rubio cautioned that Venezuelan oil alone could not cover potential global supply shortages. It could offer some relief in the short term and contribute more over time.

Share

2. Is Accenture saying goodbye to China? 👋

Accenture is reportedly exploring the sale of its Greater China business, which could be valued at up to $1.5 billion, as per Financial Times.

What’s happening: the company has hired JPMorgan to review its options after receiving interest from potential buyers over the past year. The business includes Accenture’s operations in mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Importantly, Accenture may sell a majority stake while retaining a significant minority holding.

The why: operating in China has become increasingly difficult for global consulting companies. Tighter rules around data security and sensitive information have forced several Western firms to separate their Chinese technology systems from their global networks.

The larger picture: Accenture expects revenue to grow 3-6% in FY27. It believes growth could accelerate later in the decade as more businesses move from experimenting with AI to using it across their operations.

Share

3. Big money, big donations 💸

Big AI promises now come with big giveaways. Anthropic and Elon Musk’s SpaceX have pledged a slice of their wealth as tech firms face pressure over AI’s potential impact on jobs and society. (A little goodwill certainly wouldn’t hurt)

What’s Musk offering: one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America next year. At about $150 a share, that would put the giveaway at roughly $10.8 billion for 72 million children. A hefty sum, but less than 2% of his current net worth.

SpaceX, which owns xAI, raised $85.7 billion in June in the biggest IPO in history.

And Anthropic: it has pledged 5% of its shares to a fund supporting the ‘public good’, while preparing for a potential stock market listing that could value it at over $1 trillion.

Why the generosity: the AI investment boom rests partly on the belief that businesses will get more done with fewer workers. That could boost profits while leaving employees with fewer jobs and less bargaining power, widening the gap between rich and poor.

Evidence of AI’s impact on jobs remains mixed. But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar work before the decade ends.

Share

4. How Elizabeth Holmes became Hollywood’s unlikely box-office star ⭐

Elizabeth Holmes went from building a healthcare startup once valued at $9 billion to serving an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

Now, she’s an unlikely Hollywood box-office attraction.

A new documentary, You Can See Everything, earned $15 million in its opening weekend across just 855 cinemas, with over 70% of its audience under 35.

Secretly filmed during Holmes’ final weeks before prison, it explores the woman behind the Theranos scandal and her attempts to tell her side of the story.

Watch Closely

5. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

📈 Ixigo jumped 9% while Federal Bank, Union Bank, HFCL and PNB gained up to 5% following their Q2 results.

💊 Natco Pharma rose 2% after announcing the US launch of carboplatin, a chemotherapy drug.

🏗️ JSW Steel ended more than 2% higher after the Orissa High Court quashed a ₹696 crore demand and set aside another ₹1,473 crore demand for reconsideration.

What went down ⬇️

🧹 Urban Company slipped 10% after its Q2 net loss tripled year-on-year amid spending on InstaHelp.

🏦 Jana Small Finance Bank ended 13% lower after Federal Bank said it was not in any active discussions regarding an acquisition.

📉 UltraTech Cement, HDFC Bank and Axis Bank fell up to 4% after reporting quarterly results.

🏥 Max Healthcare and other hospital stocks fell after the government capped margins on 137 cancer medicines at 30%.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

💸 Expansion mode: Vedanta doubled its South African zinc production capacity to 500,000 tonnes annually after investing nearly $600 million in Gamsberg’s expansion.

✅ Reviving shipping: Ukraine is discussing reopening Black Sea ports, its main food export route, with Turkey, Egypt and India following Russian attacks.

👀 Deal brewing: MakeMyTrip is reportedly in talks to acquire Quick Ride through redBus, potentially expanding urban mobility and strengthening corporate commute offerings.

👖Deep pockets: Premium menswear brand The Pant Project raised ₹109 crore in Series B funding to expand stores, enter new categories and strengthen omnichannel presence.

😮‍💨 Revenue record: Apple India’s FY26 revenue rose 31% to ₹1,03,853 crore, crossing ₹1 lakh crore and more than doubling its FY23 figure.

That’s a wrap! Don’t let the weekday blues get to you.

items.title: Burma Burma’s parent cooks up an IPO 😋
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks and Happy Mondayyyyy!

Before we begin, to date, we’ve sent more than 1,000 editions of Filter Coffee to your inbox, one each morning.

We’re thinking about what’s next for us: the same curiosity and personality you know, with something new in the mix.

Meanwhile, dogs can read our expressions and pick up on emotions. Could their noses also help detect cancer?

We at This Is Business spoke to Dognosis, a Bengaluru based startup exploring how dogs’ sense of smell could help spot early signs of cancer.

Co-founders Akash Kulgod and Itamar Bitan brought together research on dogs detecting disease by scent and their own experience with canine detection.

Watch our new episode and show us some 🐾 love!

And from what dogs can sniff out to what investors will be watching, here’s the week ahead on Dalal Street.

It’s a holiday-shortened week, with markets closed on Tuesday for Dussehra, but there’s still plenty to watch.

The biggest trigger will be Q2 earnings, Jio Platforms’ ₹30,000+ crore IPO, foreign investor activity, crude oil prices, the rupee-dollar movement and developments in the Middle East.

Indian IT stocks will also remain in focus after driving the market’s recent recovery.

💡 Spotlight: Cancer drug prices could fall 70% 💊

Pharma stocks including Sun Pharma, Cipla, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories and Lupin will be in focus after the government introduced new pricing rules for 137 identified non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.

As per the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), a limit has been set on the margin earned by distributors, hospitals and retailers to 30%.

These medicines were previously outside direct price controls, allowing mark-ups to average around 170% and, in some cases, rise as high as 700%.

The revised prices will take effect from November 9 and could reduce MRPs by up to 70%, depending on how each medicine is currently priced.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: Trump hits snooze on Russia sanctions ⏰

500%, 100%, then a waiver: A major turn of events appeared over the weekend after US President Donald Trump put new Russia sanctions on hold.

The waiver will remain in effect until Trump or senior administration officials determine that further action is appropriate. In simple words, the sanctions have been paused, not permanently cancelled.

Why is it significant for India: India is the world’s third-largest crude oil consumer and imports more than 88% of the oil it needs. Russia is currently its largest supplier.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that India had started diversifying its energy sources but continued to buy substantial quantities from Russia because changing suppliers could not happen overnight.

He also described India as an important US ally and partner. Rubio said the Trump administration would use up to 60 days to study how these sanctions and tariffs could affect the American and global economies.

The timing: the decision came just before the October 18 deadline for the administration to decide how the new law would be implemented.

The decision also comes weeks before the US midterm elections. Trump is facing pressure over elevated fuel prices, while the conflict with Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies.

Larger picture is Russia-Ukraine war but…

Zoom out: Trump’s decision comes shortly after he announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel.

That marked a clear shift in Washington’s approach. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, the US had focused on restricting Moscow’s energy earnings. It is now temporarily turning to Russian fuel to ease supply pressures and control prices at home.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticised the decision, arguing that easing the restrictions would help Russia continue financing the war.

Share

2. Cancer bet grows stronger 💪

Mankind Pharma has acquired a 70% stake in Belgium-based Armed Cell Therapeutics (ACTx) for €48 million (₹511 crore).

ACTx is a biotechnology company developing next-generation CAR-T therapies, which use a patient’s own immune cells to fight cancer.

Why it matters: the deal marks Mankind’s entry into CAR-T cancer therapies and supports its push to develop innovative medicines for global markets.

The acquisition, made through Mankind’s Netherlands subsidiary, gives it access to cell-therapy research capabilities and potential treatments under development for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, and small-cell lung cancer.

It also expands Mankind’s presence in Europe beyond selling medicines into biotechnology research and development.

More on acquisitions 💸,

Zen Technologies has acquired a 51.98% stake in Bengaluru-based defence technology company Cogknit Semantics for ₹135.15 crore.

What matters: Zen said the deal supports its planned AI platform, Samvid, which aims to give forces a shared view of the battlefield.

Cogknit’s battlefield management system helps connect tanks, vehicles and soldiers so they can share information and coordinate.

It is expected to work alongside Samvid and Zen Tech’s training simulators, anti-drone systems, drones and autonomous platforms.

Share

3. What’s brewing in the startup world? 🙇🏼‍♀️

Cult.fit has received SEBI’s observations on its proposed IPO. The company plans to raise ₹950 crore through a fresh issue of equity shares, alongside an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 17.86 crore shares by existing shareholders.

Some numbers: Cult.fit’s operating revenue rose 36.26% YoY to ₹1,720.61 crore in FY26, from ₹1,262.93 crore in FY25.

FYI: In November 2021, Zomato acquired a 6.4% stake in Cult.fit, helping the company achieve unicorn status at a $1.5 billion valuation.

More on IPOs,

Hunger Pangs Ltd, which owns and operates the Burma Burma restaurant chain, has filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO.

The proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of equity shares worth ₹150 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.79 crore shares by existing shareholders.

The numbers: Hunger Pangs’ revenue from operations rose 46.56% YoY to ₹156 crore in FY26, from ₹106.1 crore in FY25. However, the company posted a net loss of ₹15.3 crore during the year.

It also plans to expand its delivery and direct-to-consumer offerings, including ready-to-eat and other packaged food products.

4. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

🚀 IT index jumped nearly 4%, led by an 8% rise in Tech Mahindra after the company beat Q2 revenue expectations, aided by robust deal wins.

💻 Wipro surged nearly 6% after the company said deals deferred from Q2 were expected to close in Q3.

📊 Onward Technologies jumped 20% while Solara Active Pharma gained up to 8% after reporting Q2 results.

💍 Gems & jewellery stocks including PC Jeweller, Senco Gold and Thangamayil Jewellery saw strong buying on expectations of healthy festive demand.

🏗️ Vascon Engineers rose 11% after securing a ₹198 crore order from SBI.

What went down ⬇️

😕 Persistent Systems ended nearly 2% lower after profit came lower in Q2.

🛍️ Shoppers Stop and Cyient DLM slipped up to 13% after reporting weak Q2 earnings.

🔔 BSE fell over 2% following the revised CAS framework.

✈️ Rules finalised to regulate airfares, govt tells Supreme Court; InterGlobe Aviation down over 2%.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

items.title: U.S. banks catch AI agents going off-script
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 6,202 new readers. AI agents have been pitched as the ultimate time-saver, handling digital chores so you don’t have to. Now those same capabilities are causing headaches for America’s banking ecosystem.

Some of the top banks in the country are spotting AI agents logging into customer accounts and taking actions… And they are having a hard time telling whether it’s a user-approved agent or one going rogue.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Banks crack down on AI agents’ account access

  • Rowan’s Corner: Safeguard yourself from AI hacks

  • Put your open Chrome tabs to work

  • Microsoft’s AI out-diagnoses doctors on hard cases

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

AI AGENTS

🏦 Banks crack down on AI agents’ account access

Image source: Images 2.5 / The Rundown

The Rundown: Top U.S. banks, including JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Morgan Stanley, are restricting third-party AI agents after finding them operating inside customer accounts, with some acting beyond instructions, Axios reported.

The details:

  • The banks caught agents logging in with customers’ own credentials, against their rules, with some calling support lines or taking actions users never requested.

  • Executives called the situation “horrifying,” fearing agents might hallucinate and hit users’ finances if they’re granted authority to make purchases or move funds.

  • While most cases involved user-authorized agents, not a rogue hack, one bank executive did tell Axios that they’re struggling to tell the two apart.

  • In response, Morgan Stanley is blocking third-party agents, and JPMorgan, BofA, and Citi are restricting them, with most banks moving toward read-only access.

Why it matters: Most of the worry here comes from AI misreading instructions and acting beyond requirements, with real money at stake. With agent use growing, blanket blocks can’t last forever, but they do buy banks enough time to build frameworks that let cleared agents take defined actions and catch rogue ones (which are also growing).

TOGETHER WITH GARTNER

🔮 7 AI themes shaping the future

The Rundown: From strategy and operations to talent, technology, investment, and governance, understanding these seven AI themes helps leaders align across functions to make smarter decisions.

In this webinar, you’ll learn:

  • 7 AI themes Gartner believes will have the greatest impact over the next 12 months

  • How these themes shape risk, opportunities, and priorities

  • Key actions to respond to these shifts

Watch now.

ROWAN’S CORNER

🔒 Safeguard yourself from AI hacks

Rowan: If you’re reading this newsletter, you’re probably the most AI-literate person your family knows. That comes with a responsibility that’s worth talking about this week.

Over the past few days, we’ve seen a massive spike in malicious AI attacks, and it’s likely going to get worse (and weirder) as the internet figures out how to secure things properly. Instead of panicking, take extra precautions now.

Here’s my protection list (forward it to your family, too):

  1. Set a family code word that any caller must say before you believe an emergency, and share it in person, never over text.

  2. Hang up and call back on the number you already have saved for any urgent money request, because AI can now clone anyone’s voice from seconds of audio.

  3. Set up 2FA on your logins, preferably with an authenticator app rather than SMS.

  4. Use a good password manager (like 1Password) with zero duplicated passwords, so one leaked login can’t unlock your whole life.

  5. Update everything today (browsers, phones, laptops, desktop apps), since this week’s certificate compromise made unpatched software the open door.

  6. Confirm any payment request on a second channel, different from the one it arrived on.

If you’re a builder, I also recommend using OpenAI’s free checker to see whether your website’s PHP version is exposed to the latest vulnerability.

AI TRAINING

🌐 Put your open Chrome tabs to work

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use ChatGPT’s updated Chrome extension to compare open pages, check the facts, and group the tabs you need. Start in Chat to read, then use Work for a browser action you approve.

Step-by-step:

  1. Install the official ChatGPT extension from OpenAI and open its side panel. Use a practice Chrome profile with public pages for your first run

  2. Open three pricing pages and tell ChatGPT which tabs to read. Give it your team size, required features, budget, and billing period

  3. Check the comparison against the pages. Confirm the full team cost and leave missing details unverified rather than guessing

  4. Switch to Work where available and ask it to group only those three tabs. Review the list first, then check the actual group in Chrome

  5. Ask for a short recommendation with source links and one question to resolve. Keep trials, purchases, and messages outside the task

Pro tip: A monthly price paid once a year is not a month-to-month offer. Check the billing label before comparing totals. Pro members get the comparison brief, prompt cards, and review checklist.

PRESENTED BY GRANOLA

🗓️ Your meetings, slides included

The Rundown: Granola is the AI notepad for people with back-to-back meetings. With Snapshots, you can save what’s shared on screen in a call to your notes. Later, ask about the meeting and the slide comes up with the answer.

Granola now lets you:

  • Save slides, dashboards, and docs from calls

  • Keep slides with your meeting notes

  • Find the slide when you need it

Get your first month on us with code THERUNDOWN.

AI RESEARCH

🩺 Microsoft’s AI out-diagnoses doctors on hard cases

Image source: Microsoft AI

The Rundown: Microsoft just published initial results from its MAI-DxO AI diagnostic system, revealing that it beats physicians on both complex medical cases and everyday ER visits while ordering fewer, cheaper tests at the same time.

The details:

  • MAI-DxO works like a virtual panel of doctors, with AI agents proposing diagnoses, ordering tests, and challenging each other as new results come in.

  • On 304 complex ‘New England Journal of Medicine’ cases, it more than doubled physicians’ accuracy with reference tools; on typical ER cases, it hit 80% vs. 47%.

  • One setup reached 81% accuracy on the NEJM cases at less than half the cost of comparable systems, with the gains holding even with newer models like GPT-5.5.

  • Microsoft will test the system in real clinical settings at Beth Israel Deaconess in Boston, measuring how its patient diagnoses fare against clinicians’ assessments.

Why it matters: Microsoft’s ER findings make a strong case for AI in diagnosis, but getting the assessment right is only one step in care. For AI to truly help patients, it will also need to guide treatment, track health over time, and fit into how doctors and patients make decisions together, all of which still have to be proven at scale.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Ben built a live task dashboard with a Raspberry Pi and Claude

Today’s workflow comes from reader Ben Blay:

I built a module that runs in MagicMirror on a Raspberry Pi and displays a real-time to-do list on a television in my office.

Claude does an admirable job managing my daily task list, which is stored in TASKS.md on my local computer. I wanted an at-a-glance dashboard showing everything I have in progress, sorted by priority and synchronized with that file.

I described the goal to Claude Code. Since I already had an old Raspberry Pi 3 and an off-the-shelf widescreen TV in my office, Claude Code suggested running MagicMirror on the Pi and Syncthing on both the Pi and my local computer to keep the file updated.

Claude then built the MagicMirror module to read TASKS.md. After a few tweaks to remove the default modules and clean up the spacing between items, the display was up and running. I set MagicMirror to start automatically when the Pi boots, so now my to-do list is in front of me all day.

AI infra company Baseten released two free open-source decision models, mammoth-1 and elephant-1, with mammoth ranking #1 on the Jev Decision Index.

OpenAI is nearing a funding round of up to $30B at a $1.25T valuation, led by UAE investors, CNBC reported, citing people familiar with the deal.

Ex-OpenAI executive Kevin Weil’s Warp Sciences raised $215M Series A to build AI- and robotics-powered labs to help drugmakers develop medicines faster in the U.S.

items.title: AI finds a security hole in 70% of the web

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 15,837 new readers. Just months ago, GPT-5.6 Sol made headlines for hacking Hugging Face. Now, the same model is on the other side of the fence, catching “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

OpenAI’s last-gen model helped researchers identify two critical flaws in PHP, the code behind about 70% of the web, sending IT teams worldwide into scramble mode — and the company says it has more major security finds like this still waiting to be disclosed.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws

  • Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI

🚨 OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws

Image source: X / The Rundown

The Rundown: PHP, the coding language behind ~70% of websites, just pushed patches for two critical flaws caught with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, with the National Security Agency urging anyone who can’t patch right away to pull systems offline.

The details:

  • Security firm Calif found the first bug on Aug. 1 using 5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz separately caught both weeks later with Sol and Gemini 4 Argon.

  • OpenAI said it worked on patches alongside the PHP maintainers for two months, calling the find “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

  • The decade-old bugs let hackers hijack servers with no login, and OpenAI calls them two of “several significant vulnerabilities” it’s still fixing.

  • Governments in Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands pulled websites offline, with Cloudflare saying it was “seeing early attacks emerging.”

Why it matters: PHP is used on 70% of websites, making the scale of this vulnerability massive — and yet it wasn’t turned into a working attack until a model now far behind the frontier was pointed at it. Pre-AI code is far more fragile than anyone imagined, and the only hope is that the good guys (and AI) can stay a step ahead of the exploits.

TOGETHER WITH GOOGLE FOR STARTUPS

💼 Gemini 4 Argon founder briefing

The Rundown: Google Cloud invites startup founders to an exclusive briefing with the Google DeepMind team to break down the newly announced Gemini 4 Argon model, exploring game-changing use cases and technical enhancements.

  • DeepMind's perspective on high-impact startup use cases

  • Direct, unfiltered Q&A with the DeepMind team

Register for the briefing.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK

🔌 Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: If AI still isn’t making you faster, look at where your time goes. You’re searching for the right email, attaching the doc, compiling the context it needs. Then, once the work’s done, you’re copying and pasting everything it made back into the places it belongs.

My rule: if it’s as simple as a copy and paste, AI should be doing it for you through a connector.

Connectors also clear the nice-to-do pile. Everyone has a survey they’ve been meaning to send. It’s the kind of finishing touch that takes good work to great, and the first thing to go when we’re squished.

Hook your AI up to Tally or Jotform, and the whole loop happens without leaving chat: brainstorm the questions, build the form, draft the email to your audience, then pull the responses back in and make sense of them. Not a survey person? Find the finishing touch that lives in one or two tools you could connect today.

I sat on the sidelines over security, too. Now my ladder is read, then write, then send. Surveys are a safe first rung; nothing goes out by accident. Draft and critique everything in chat first. When it touches your inbox, it writes the draft, and you hit send.

Online banking felt risky too, until one day you stopped going to the branch. By next fall, most of us won’t open our inbox first. Our agent will have already triaged it and pitched us a short list of projects to say yes or no to.

Which app would you let your AI read first: inbox, drive, or calendar?

AI TRAINING

🗓️ Let Town prepare your next meeting brief

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Town, a business-focused personal AI assistant, to turn email and calendar details into a meeting brief. You’ll catch an unconfirmed time change, check the open work, and save the process for reuse.

Step-by-step:

  1. Sign up for Town and connect an approved Google test account. Keep changes behind approval and review any routines already running

  2. Add the guide’s fictional emails and private calendar event. Ask your Townie to read those exact sources and prepare a short brief in the conversation

  3. Check the meeting time, launch date, budget, and open tasks. A request to move a meeting should stay separate from the time still on the calendar

  4. Update the test event and send the confirming email. Ask for a fresh brief and check that only the changed facts move with it

  5. Save the process as a routine that runs only when you choose. Inspect its tools, delivery, and first result before adding a daily schedule

Pro tip: Town’s read-only routines can still email reports to you. Check the recipient and delivery settings as well as the mode. Pro members get the practice emails, prompts, and answer key.

PRESENTED BY VANTA

🍀 Spoiler: it wasn’t luck

The Rundown: Competition’s tough for startups, and everyone needs an edge. Nothing kills a deal faster than showing up without a SOC 2, but audit prep takes time most teams don’t have. Vanta gets you SOC 2-ready fast.

See for yourself:

  • 20% shorter enterprise deal cycles

  • $1.5M in sales unlocked in 3 months

  • SOC 2 Type II readiness in 3 weeks

Request a demo.

ANTHROPIC

🤖 Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet

Image source: Anthropic / The Rundown

The Rundown: Anthropic just introduced Claude Duet, an Opus 5.5-powered personal agent standalone app that can take proactive actions, work 24/7 (even when closed), and carry out tasks on its own cloud computer.

The details:

  • Example tasks include morning briefs, tracking calendars, and booking meetings, with Duet able to use its own computer even when devices are off.

  • Duet carries over memory, skills, and connectors from the Claude app, and also gains payment functionality via a one-time virtual card from Stripe’s Link wallet.

  • Anthropic put a focus on security and safety for Duet, with any deletion, payment, signature, or outgoing message needing user sign-off first.

  • Duet conversations count as part of normal Claude usage limits, with the research preview rolling out in waves to waitlisted U.S. Max and Pro subscribers.

Why it matters: The personal agent trend is already overflowing, and we’d agree… With this one exception. Anthropic’s models are in a class of their own right now, and while Grok Bot already borrows Claude for some tasks, Duet is the only one built entirely around Opus 5.5 — a model so good it could be the edge that separates it from the pack.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Shimon built an AI donor tracker that flags who hasn’t given yet

Today’s workflow comes from reader Shimon:

“I built an AI fundraising campaign assistant with Make.com. The workflow reads emails sent from the crowdfunding platform used for the campaign, extracts the relevant information, and records it in a spreadsheet.

It also uses spreadsheets from previous years’ campaigns to maintain a list of people who have not donated to this campaign yet but have donated in the past. I can ask the agent questions by email, such as who has already donated. It can also answer questions with specific parameters, such as who has not donated but previously gave more than $1,000, or how much a specific person donated.

I built the workflow in Make using its AI tools. I connected it to a Gmail account, a Google Drive account containing the spreadsheets, and a ChatGPT account that processes the information as the AI agent.”

items.content:

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,761 new readers. OpenAI’s current AI safety playbook — shipping models once they pass safety tests and flagging any concerns — is what Sam Altman reportedly calls “pacing 1.0.” The sequel options are a bit more extreme.

Altman reportedly gave staff three possible outcomes: a global watchdog, a single super-lab merger, or one lab racing ahead to “melt everyone else’s GPUs,” an outcome he called “terrible.” OpenAI now has a year to choose its own path.

Reminder: Our next live workshop is today at 12 PM EST — join and learn how to get the most out of Microsoft Copilot and leverage its newest features to get real work done. RSVP here.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Sam Altman details the AI industry’s endgame

  • Anthropic’s Claude takes on scorpion antivenom

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI

🔮 Sam Altman details the AI industry’s endgame

Image source: Images 2.5 / The Rundown

The Rundown: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman gave an internal talk to staff last week that covered three possible endgames for safe AI, according to The Information — ranging from a global watchdog combining the top labs to one company racing ahead.

The details:

  • The report claims Altman favored plan 1: a global enforcer built like the International Atomic Energy Agency, which OAI has lobbied for since 2023.

  • The “Demis plan” (named after DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis) folds top labs into one lab serving partner countries, similar to CERN’s particle research.

  • Altman called plan three (named for AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky) “terrible,” with one lab riding self-improving AI to “melt everyone else’s GPUs.”

  • He called picking a path, due within a year, “pacing 2.0,” and said it must include a “speed limit” or stopping point for self-improving AI.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s Jack Clark just talked about an intelligence cap and said the world has “a small number of years” to act on safety — and Altman’s scenarios seem aligned with his No. 1 rival. An Avengers-style team-up of top labs under one roof would make for a fun plot, but as with every pact so far, getting the rest of the field is not easy.

TOGETHER WITH PAVE

🏗️ Build customized, connected apps in minutes

🏭 Ex-OpenAI research chief’s Arda debuts at $1.5B

The Rundown: Former OpenAI Chief Research Officer Bob McGrew just came out of stealth with Arda, a startup building AI that helps factories set up assembly lines for new products far faster, launching at a $1.5B valuation after a $160M Series A round.

The details:

  • McGrew pitched Arda as being able to do “for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers,” planning builds from design files.

  • The comparison is Asia’s factories, where big crews relearn a new design in a day, while reprogramming one automated station can cost nearly $1M.

  • Defense firm Anduril, Arda’s first customer, says basic assembly instructions now take 15 minutes vs. 10 hours, and it’d be “behind” without the tech.

  • McGrew wants robots on the line next, reprogrammed by Arda’s agents in days, calling the goal “a fully automated version of Shenzhen in West Texas.”

Why it matters: McGrew joins Mira Murati, Ilya Sutskever, and others on the list of OAI departures now running billion-dollar startups, but Arda is the rare one building factories instead of frontier models. It also comes months after Jeff Bezos’ Prometheus raised $12B for an “artificial general engineer,” focusing on designing physical products.

AI TRAINING

🪝 Make Claude Code check its work after each edit

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll make Claude Code format a settings file and run checks after selected edits. You’ll introduce a small error, see which test catches it, and fix the code without changing the test.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open a new practice folder and ask Claude to build the guide’s small shipping calculator. Run the five tests to check that it works before adding a hook

  2. Add a hook that formats the settings file after Claude writes it. Save the settings on a line and check the hook makes them easier to read without changing values

  3. Add the shipping tests to the same hook. Have it finish formatting before running the checks, then confirm all five pass

  4. Ask Claude to introduce the guide’s deliberate error. An order worth exactly $50 should now fail the free-shipping test. Read the failure before fixing anything

  5. Restore the original rule and run the same tests again. Check that all five pass, then follow the guide’s steps to turn the hook off

Pro tip: Keep the tests unchanged while fixing the bug. This hook checks an edit after it saves, so a failed check leaves the change in place. Our Pro members get the prepared hook, practice files, and tests.

PRESENTED BY GLEAN

💰 Bad AI architecture ate your token budget

The Rundown: For enterprise leaders scaling AI, Glean delivers more useful work per token — because better context, smart model routing, and efficient agent design cut waste before the model ever spends a token.

In this story, you’ll see:

  • How a context layer reduces wasted processing

  • Why model routing sends tasks to the right model

  • How Glean saves 81% fewer tokens per task vs. Claude Coworker

Explore the full story to calculate potential savings.

AI & DRUG DISCOVERY

🦂 Anthropic’s Claude takes on scorpion antivenom

Image source: Citrini

The Rundown: Anthropic published new research in which an internal AI designed proteins to lock onto scorpion venom toxins and disarm them, run with the investment firm Citrini Research, with two outside labs confirming that 17 of 211 designs worked.

The details:

  • Citrini’s five staffers worked at Anthropic’s offices after they couldn’t get the safety block lifted on their own computers, with an estimated budget of $200,000.

  • Claude ran for 64 hours off five human messages, drawing up 318,484 candidate designs and sending 211 to Twist Bioscience and Adaptyv Bio for lab work.

  • 17 designs passed the binding tests, but each grabs only one toxin, and the proteins haven’t been tested to see if they can actually stop the venom.

  • Citrini declared its moonshot experiment of a universal antivenom ‘failed’, but its takeaway was that the “frontier has moved” for AI and drug discovery.

Why it matters: Claude is designing protein binders and working in its own lab, but the key here is who was holding the keyboard — staffers from an investment newsletter with a $200K budget and no deep drug development experience. Factor in constantly improving AI, and the pipeline for creating scientific research is looking very different.

items.title: Anthropic co-founder says the singularity is underway
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,481 new readers. Anthropic has spent 2026 warning that AI is moving faster than anyone is ready for. Now one of its co-founders says the moment has a name.

Jack Clark just said that the singularity, when AI-driven progress starts outrunning humanity’s ability to keep up, is officially underway. What comes with it? A possible $44T U.S. economy, serious job disruption, and a short window to decide if AI needs an intelligence cap.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Anthropic co-founder says the singularity is underway

  • One hacker’s AI agents break into 100+ companies

  • Try ChatGPT’s new voices with GPT-Live-1.1

  • Inception’s Mercury 3 speeds past rivals

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

ANTHROPIC

🌌 Anthropic co-founder says the singularity is underway

Image source: IMF

The Rundown: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark just told economists and policymakers at the IMF and World Bank’s annual meetings that the singularity, the point where AI speeds up discovery faster than humans can follow, has “now begun.”

The details:

  • Clark pointed to AI’s scores on Humanity’s Last Exam (expert-level questions) going from 8% to 67.7% since 2025, and FrontierMath improving from 2% to 94%.

  • One Anthropic model has U.S. GDP at $44T by 2030 if AI spreads fast, which Clark admitted sounds outlandish but also predicts “very disruptive” job impacts.

  • The world’s 10M scientists may soon direct “a billion virtual scientists,” Clark said while urging nations to build labs and robots before they run short.

  • He also said CEO Dario Amodei has floated limits on AI’s “ceiling of intelligence,” adding that he believes there is only “a small number of years” to act.

Why it matters: With the number of AI math and science breakthroughs in the last few months alone, 2026 has handed Clark plenty of evidence. Singularity talk used to live strictly in science fiction, and now one of the people building it is saying it out loud to the folks who run the global economy.

TOGETHER WITH ATLASSIAN

📈 AI adoption has outpaced strategy

The Rundown: Atlassian’s 2026 State of the Developer Experience report, based on global research with 1,560 respondents including devs and engineering leaders, maps out clear paths for leaders to help their teams manage the speed vs. friction tension happening right now.

In the report, you’ll explore how:

  • Devs are managing more output

  • An AI-native SDLC fixes bottlenecks

  • Only 23% of leaders have an AI strategy

Download the full State of DevEx 2026 Report today.

AI & SECURITY

🔓 One hacker’s AI agents break into 100+ companies

Image source: NorForge

The Rundown: Security firm NorForge revealed that a Chinese-speaking hacker let AI agents do nearly all the work to successfully break into the websites of 100+ companies, with Reuters identifying victims like Cummins, Deere, and SharkNinja in the hack.

The details:

  • NorForge watched the attacks after finding 20+ hacker control panels for Cairn, an open-source tool for AI agents, left online with no password.

  • The hacker fed the agents a pre-screened list of busy online stores and orders under 100 Chinese characters, then sent them after over 1,200 sites.

  • NorForge puts AI costs near $50 per successful break-in, with a typical one taking nearly a day using Claude Code and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

  • It’s unclear if any data was taken, with SharkNinja calling the threat contained, Deere citing “remediation actions,” and Cummins “investigating.”

Why it matters: A month ago, we were writing about “three guys with Claude” breaking into OpenAI, and now it’s one hacker with an estimated $5K in tokens and a short note to their agents hitting 100+ companies. AI’s offensive cyber capabilities are outpacing the defensive ones, and a lot of companies are about to be caught in the crosshairs.

AI TRAINING

🎙️ Try ChatGPT’s new voices with GPT-Live-1.1

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try ChatGPT’s new voices, compare them with the same short passage, and check whether a spoken correction reaches the final answer.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open ChatGPT’s Voice settings and choose Live where available. Pick a voice and start a new chat with the guide’s fictional workshop notice

  2. Ask it to read the notice, then try the same words with another voice. Keep the language and instructions fixed so the comparison stays useful

  3. Try a regional voice in a language you know well. Listen for clear names, dates, and numbers, and ask for a slower repeat when needed

  4. Interrupt the notice with a new date and headcount. Check that those details change while the time and budget stay fixed

  5. Ask Voice to search OpenAI’s release notes. Open its source link and check the answer rather than trusting the spoken search cue alone

Pro tip: A new voice and a new model are different changes. Comparing Bubbie with your usual voice does not prove a gain over GPT-Live-1. Pro members get the practice prompts and listening checklist.

PRESENTED BY OPTIMIZELY

🤖 Find high-value AI use cases

The Rundown: Most AI planning starts with the wrong question. Instead of asking “What should AI do?”, ask “Where does the work break?” Optimizely’s template helps you identify high-value AI use cases by finding the manual work slowing you down.

This template gives you:

  • A personalized AI use case in minutes

  • The same process that turned a 2-3 hour GA4 reporting task into a 5-minute one

  • A use case mapped to how your team actually works, not a generic list of ideas

Download the template.

INCEPTION

⚡️ Inception’s Mercury 3 speeds past rivals

Image source: Inception

The Rundown: AI startup Inception just launched Mercury 3, a “diffusion” language model it says matches or beats OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 by its own numbers at 4-8x their speed.

The details:

  • Language models write one at a time, while diffusion models draft many words at once and refine them, leading to outputs of 1,000+ tokens a second.

  • Inception pitches it as useful for apps where any lag shows, with early users running live tutors, voice customer support, and web-browsing agents on it.

  • Mercury 3 is priced at $0.20/$0.70 per million tokens, with the company saying the model is 40x the size of Mercury 1 while still maintaining the same speeds.

  • Co-founder Stefano Ermon said scaling diffusion is limited by “compute and data, not fundamental algorithmic barriers,” and a successor is already in training.

Why it matters: Mercury 3 won’t replace the frontier AI people use for hard reasoning, and Inception isn’t pretending it will. But with OpenAI’s Cerebras partnership and a new Ultrafast tier that pushes GPT-6 Astra as high as 300 tokens/s, speed is clearly the next battleground — and Inception is betting an alternative model type can win it.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ A reader built a voice-enabled task management system with Claude

Today’s workflow comes from an anonymous Rundown reader:

I’m 78, and I run a homestead, a home server, and a senior center, with dozens of jobs underway at once. Most jobs get done a piece at a time, while to-do apps only track whether something is “done” or “not done.”

So I built Taskmaster: a plain-text ledger inside a Claude Project. I first tried building a large custom app, then scrapped it. One of my own rules is, “Build the ugly version first.”

In the field, I speak notes into the Claude app on my phone. Claude saves my exact words, updates each job’s progress, and asks me one question at a time when something is unclear. When I ask, “What’s next?” it considers deadlines, weather, and my energy level, then gives me one to three things to do.

Anything tied to a specific time goes on my Google Calendar. Home Assistant then reads the reminder aloud through my hearing aids. Today, it checked the forecast and scheduled my paint job for the one day this week that stays above 50°F overnight. The machine carries the complexity, so I don’t have to.
